text.p: The level of success of the proposed merger between Conrail Inc and CSX Corp will likely depend on how much competitive access the merged firm must grant along its key North-South routes, analysts said.

Analysts interviewed after the merger announcement also said an expected delay in earnings gains from the merger has weighed on CSX's stock price since the deal was announced, and the $8.4 billion to be paid for Conrail would represent a premium over other recent rail mergers.
But this deal may be the last big one for now in a wave of consolidation in the rail industry, the analysts said.
"You could always look for an East-West merger...but I don't think that's immediate," said PNC Institutional Investment Services analyst Charles Vincent.

Prudential Securities analyst Brian Routledge said CSX was paying about 10 times earnings before interest and taxes for Conrail, compared with prices of about eight to nine times earnings in other recent rail mergers. Asked whether the deal were worth the premium, he said earlier rail industry mergers have shown significant benefits could be gained from a merger.

"How quickly they realize those benefits will depend on how much access they have to give up to competing railroads in the regulatory process, and we won't know that until probably late next year," Routledge said.

Approval from the federal Surface Transportation Board is required for the merger to take place. Analysts said approval was likely, but the board would probably seek to make sure there was a competitive environment. Norfolk Southern Corp -- which was in late 1994 rumored to be in merger talks with Conrail -- said the proposed merger raised concerns regarding the transportation system and shipping public.

CSX Chairman John Snow said in a telephone news conference that he and Conrail Chairman David LeVan intended to "sit down with our counterparts at Norfolk Southern...and see if we can't accomodate their concerns."
CSX and Conrail said in announcing their merger that they were willing to grant competitive access on track where the two companies are now the only competitors.
Snow alluded to trackage rights granted by combined firms in earlier mergers. "We could see a constructive dialogue with (Norfolk Southern) evolving in that direction," Snow said.

Routledge said CSX's share price was down on Tuesday partly in reaction to its statement the deal would not be accretive to earnings until the second year of the merger, which is expected to be completed in late 1997.

The analysts agreed with CSX and Conrail that major benefits of the merger would be in combining Conrail's Northeast routes with CSX's Southeast ones to provide shippers in the eastern United States with a single rail company serving North-South routes, a market now dominated by the trucking industry.
LeVan said the firms projected increased traffic would boost operating income about $200 million annually.
CSX and Conrail executives in the conference call said they had no estimate of the total North-South shipping market, or the share of it now held by the trucking industry.
However, Snow said the trucking industry has roughly a $300 billion annual market in the United States, against about $30 billion for rail.
Separately, the two companies said in information on the merger that two-thirds of all North American trucking tonnage passes through the Eastern United States.
